repo: lottie-web (baseline that dotLottie Web is compared against)
quality_note: Crisp Skia vector edges at 1080 and 2160 (edge spread 2.15 px, hairline contrast 44), gradients smooth, trim-path draw-on correct. Minus one: Trim-before-Repeater renders ticks shorter than the keyframes say (and than ThorVG); drop-shadow effect is clipped to a hard box.
unique: The native HyperFrames Lottie adapter drives it with zero glue; the reference implementation for AE exports (full build also runs AE expressions).
why: Default Lottie player for HyperFrames: works through the native adapter with 3 lines; its only gate miss is G2 at 84.9 dB (1 to 3 pixels on a 22 %-alpha hairline at frames 6, 10, 11), i.e. Chrome SVG raster noise of the same class that makes the inline-SVG draw-on render byte-different at -w 1 vs -w 2.

quality_note: Edges as crisp as SVG, but the canvas renderer ignores effects (drop shadow, fill), ignores animated gradient-stroke width, applies group opacity per item (fill and stroke blend through each other) and drops sub-pixel trim slivers (frame 37).
why: Same speed as the SVG renderer, strictly fewer features, and it renders a BLANK video in HyperFrames unless its container has an explicit pixel size (HyperFrames stamps the root size after inline scripts run).

licence: MIT (ThorVG inside the wasm is MIT too)
quality_note: ThorVG matches lottie-web within ~50 dB on shapes, strokes and gradients and follows the keyframe maths where lottie-web does not (Trim before Repeater); proper blurred drop shadow, Fill effect and simple expressions work; sharp at 2160 when the canvas follows devicePixelRatio. Minus one: edges a little softer than Skia in the HyperFrames 4K path (2.9 vs 2.25 px edge spread) and a corner artefact on a rotated 8x8 PNG magnified 17x (clean at 1:1, 3x and 0.5x with a 128 px PNG, where its image edges are smoother than lottie-web).
unique: Software raster (WASM) into a bitmap: byte-identical mp4 for -w 1 and -w 2 (tested; stable across machines is expected from the CPU-only raster but untested); .lottie bundles (1,506 B vs 5,870 B JSON, bit-identical frames); effects and expressions that lottie-web SVG draws badly; 32 % cheaper per frame at 2160 in the screenshot harness (110 vs 162 ms), which does not show up in the HyperFrames capture (5.4 vs 6.1 s for 60 frames at square-4k).
why: Use it for .lottie bundles, effect-heavy files (drop shadow, fill) and when byte-reproducible renders matter; needs a 7-line hf-seek bridge because the native HyperFrames adapter silently renders a blank video for it.

quality_note: Every frame of the HyperFrames render is the empty background (PSNR 10.9 to 11.8 dB against the correct frames): the adapter finds neither setCurrentRawFrameValue nor seek on DotLottie and does nothing, with no warning.
why: The integration the HyperFrames docs describe (register the player on window.__hfLottie) renders blank for current dotlottie-web; use the hf-seek bridge instead.

quality_note: Same picture as the software build (47.8 dB median between them; only the sliver frame 37 differs strongly).
why: Passes all three gates headless under ANGLE-Metal but adds a GPU raster dependency for no visible gain; the software build is bit-stable and fast enough. Not rendered through HyperFrames.

quality_note: Crisp Canvas2D vector at 1920x1080 and at 3840x2160 (DPR 2 canvas); the sample truck/idle animation looks as the Rive samples do.
why: Seeks deterministically (instance.time = 0; advance(t); apply(1); artboard.advance(0)) and renders in HyperFrames through a 15-line hf-seek bridge, but we cannot author .riv files, the runtime is 2.0 MB raw, and state machines need fixed-step replay: not worth a place in the default stack.

quality_note: A state machine seeks deterministically only by replaying from a fresh instance in fixed steps (n x 1/fps from 0, input fired at a fixed step). The frame at the same t differs between a 30 fps and a 60 fps step (31.7 to 38.8 dB) and between n small steps and one big advance (19.9 to 24.8 dB).
why: Pure function of t only for a fixed canonical step; changing the output fps or step changes the picture, and cost grows with t.
